analysis.one_liner: Doubles the window to pursue child labor cases and requires yearly public reports on violations.
analysis.headline: The bipartisan bill died in committee without a hearing, vote, or any Senate action beyond referral.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would amend the Fair Labor Standards Act, the nation's core wage-and-hour law, to strengthen child labor enforcement. It changes a 30-day period in the law's child labor provision to 90 days, and it requires the Labor Department to report to Congress every year on child labor violations: how many complaints, investigations, and violations occurred, which industries they happened in, how many children were involved, and whether any child was killed or seriously hurt. The idea was to make the scale of illegal child hiring visible and to give enforcers more time to act.
analysis.who_benefits: Children and teenagers under 18 who are illegally employed in hazardous or excessive work, and the public, which gains an annual, industry-by-industry accounting of where child labor violations happen. Longer enforcement windows also help workers and prosecutors build cases after violations are discovered.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Children in illegal or hazardous jobs

how_it_helps.text: Requires the Labor Department to submit an annual report to Congress detailing complaints, open and closed investigations, the number of child labor violations, breakdowns by industry, the ages and sexes of child employees involved, violations that caused death or serious injury, and penalties assessed.
Amends Section 12(a) of the Fair Labor Standards Act by striking 'thirty' and inserting '90', extending a 30-day period in the child labor provision to 90 days, giving enforcers more time.
Requires the report to include criminal charges and convictions for illegally employing oppressing children, and to describe trends and recommend steps to Congress for combating violations.

analysis.who_pays: Employers who use illegal child labor, in industries such as meatpacking and food processing where violations surged in recent years, would face longer exposure to enforcement and public reporting of their industries' violation records.
analysis.who_pays_short: Employers relying on illegal child labor

drawbacks.text: The bill's main tool is transparency, not teeth: it does not raise civil fines or add new inspectors, so it could produce detailed annual reports on violations without changing how many children are illegally employed.
The underlying law change is narrow, converting a 30-day period to 90 days, so its practical effect on enforcement is limited compared with broader child labor crackdowns proposed elsewhere.

An honest supporter would acknowledge that more reporting and enforcement paperwork imposes compliance costs on legitimate employers of teenagers, and that annual reporting alone does not prevent injuries.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The costs are modest: some compliance paperwork and longer enforcement exposure for employers, with no new fines or mandates on ordinary workers or families. The benefits are real but modest too, since the bill adds enforcement time and mandatory public reporting rather than tougher penalties or more investigators. A well-designed bill would have paired the reporting with higher penalties; as written, it is a low-cost step toward accountability rather than a fix.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate HELP committee, and nothing ever happened after that — no hearing, no vote, and the Congress ended with it still sitting in committee.

narrative.text: Sen. Marco Rubio introduced the bill on October 26, 2023, joined by Senators Padilla, Hickenlooper, and Marshall at introduction.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions, its only committee action.
Six senators cosponsored the bill: five of 48 Senate Democrats and one of 49 Senate Republicans.
No further action appears in the bill's record before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who rely on illegal child labor are better off, since the bill's annual public reporting on violations by industry and its extended enforcement window never took effect. Children illegally employed in hazardous jobs gained nothing.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had bipartisan sponsorship — a Republican lead sponsor with five Democratic and one Republican cosponsor — and no vote ever occurred, so the partisan shape of the opposition is unknown.

industries.industry: Meatpacking and food processing employers and their contractors
industries.note: These industries were at the center of a surge in child labor violations, including minors on overnight cleaning crews in meat plants. The bill would have exposed their violation records publicly each year and given enforcers more time to pursue cases.

industries.industry: Agricultural and low-wage service employers of minors
industries.note: Any employer illegally employing children would face longer enforcement exposure and industry-level reporting of violations. Lawful employers of teens would bear only modest compliance costs.
Annual public reporting on violations, injuries, and deaths involving child workers, plus a longer enforcement window, would strengthen protections for children at work.
